banner.text: Edith, 82, in bed at an assisted living home, hot to the touch, picking at the sheets, not making sense.
Edith is working harder to breathe; wet crackles at both bases.

objective: Recognize sepsis and septic shock and begin fluids early

sources.cite: NASEMSO. National Model EMS Clinical Guidelines, Version 3.0 (March 2022): Shock
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the full text Iowa HHS hosts (https://hhs.iowa.gov/media/198/download) through summarizing fetches with quotes; NASEMSO's own page, read the same day, still presents Version 3 (2022) as current and names no later version. Septic shock: early IV fluid in rapid predetermined boluses up to 30 mL/kg, stopping at the MAP goal (65 mmHg) or if pulmonary edema develops; withhold further fluid if the patient worsens or rales develop; vasopressors only when shock does not respond to fluid; advance notice to the hospital.

sources.note: Read 2026-11-17: the record page (title, report number, date; the change notices add intramuscular injection, vaccination in a public health emergency and nasal swab collection at EMT and above) and the PDF's skill tables through a summarizing fetch whose table columns were partly unclear, so placement was checked against the course's own reading (backend/supabase/seed/labs/ems-sources.ts, 2026-11-09) and REQ-241's reading (2026-11-11). EMR: oxygen, BVM, naloxone (intranasal or auto-injector), unit-dose hazmat antidote auto-injectors, tourniquet, wound packing, emergency moves, manual stabilization; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, oral glucose, aspirin, the patient's own nitroglycerin, an inhaled bronchodilator, CPAP, the epinephrine auto-injector. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways, waveform capnography, sublingual nitroglycerin and a limited list of IV and IM drugs (dextrose, naloxone). Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing, needle chest decompression, intubation and medicated infusions. No newer model was found on 2026-11-17.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

Her mean arterial pressure (60 at first) rising about 3 mmHg per 500 mL bolus, and the rule that more than 1,500 mL given without a lung check, or more than 2,000 mL in all, brings pulmonary edema in this 60 kg woman, are authored FLAG figures; NASEMSO gives up to 30 mL/kg in boluses toward a MAP of 65, stopping for pulmonary edema. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

brief.situation: 03:20. You are a paramedic with an EMT partner, called to an assisted living home: Edith, 82, about 60 kg, has been 'off' since yesterday and is now confused and hot. Staff say she has had a cough.
handover: You carry a monitor with capnography, IV supplies and normal saline, oxygen and a glucometer.
The emergency department is 15 minutes away.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Every assessment and treatment takes the time it would on a real call. Scene time and the drive run on the clock.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends when care is handed over, then a debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Why sepsis, why fluids, and what would make you stop?

parts.label: Hypotheses
parts.criteria: Fever, confusion, a fast breathing rate, low pressure (MAP about 60) and a likely source (pneumonia): septic shock; glucose excludes hypoglycemia; consider other causes of confusion.
parts.modelAnswer: Fever 39.2, new confusion, breathing 26, MAP 60 and a productive cough with right-base crackles: septic shock from pneumonia. Glucose 142 rules out a low.

parts.label: Fluids and limits
parts.criteria: Early boluses (500 mL here) toward a MAP of 65, up to 30 mL/kg (about 1.8 L for 60 kg), reassessing lungs and work of breathing between boluses; stop for new crackles or pulmonary edema; sepsis alert.
parts.modelAnswer: 500 mL boluses toward a MAP of 65, about 30 mL/kg at most, checking her lungs between each; new crackles mean stop. Sepsis alert so the team is ready.

noProgress.rationale: She arrived still below the MAP goal; fluids came late or too little.

expertPath.text: Hot, confused, fast breathing, cough: monitor, BP (MAP 60), temperature, glucose, capnography, oxygen.
Two IVs; 500 mL bolus; sepsis alert; load.
Lungs after each bolus; repeat to MAP 65, about 30 mL/kg at most; stop for new crackles.

resus.headline: Early fluids with a stop rule
resus.body: Septic shock from pneumonia: boluses toward a MAP of 65, lungs checked between each, and a sepsis alert.

arrived.headline: Arrived, by a harder route
arrived.body: Check the MAP at arrival, the lung checks and the alert.

edema.headline: Fluids need a stop rule
edema.body: Litres without listening gave her pulmonary edema. Reassess between boluses.

dry.headline: Septic shock needs fluid
dry.body: Age is not a reason to withhold early fluids; it is a reason to reassess often.

scoring.modelReasoning: Fever, new confusion, a fast breathing rate, MAP 60 and a productive cough: septic shock from pneumonia; glucose rules out hypoglycemia. Oxygen titrated, two IVs, early isotonic boluses (500 mL) toward a MAP of 65, up to about 30 mL/kg, with the lungs and work of breathing checked between boluses and fluids stopped for new crackles (NASEMSO). Sepsis alert to the ED; vasopressors are for shock that does not respond to fluid.
